input.subject: Direct a short AI-generated story: plan and produce coherent 8-10 second video clips that hold together on their own and chain into a sequence with consistent character, space, and light.
input.entryReader: Has typed a prompt into an AI video generator and gotten a clip back. Has never planned a shot, chained two clips, or kept a character consistent across generations.
input.notGiven: No page count, no outline, and no existing page content are inputs to this run.
input.capabilitiesVerified: Tool capability claims below were checked against the generators' own documentation on 2026-09-26; this area changes monthly and every claim is dated.

perspectives.view: A clip is a shot, and a shot is one idea. Framing, camera motivation, and the axis are decided before anything is generated; the model is the camera, not the director.

Capabilities differ per generator and change monthly: who anchors a first frame, who takes start and end keyframes, who extends with full-clip context, who accepts reference images and how many. Check the docs, date the claim.
Continuity is assembled, not generated: end frames become start frames, short clips stitch better than long ones, and the cut hides the seam when something moves across it.

concepts.name: Container versus prose
concepts.summary: Resolution, duration, and aspect are parameters set in the tool, not wishes in the prompt. Prose controls subject, motion, lighting, and style; it cannot make a clip longer.

concepts.name: One beat per clip
concepts.summary: The 8-10 second length forces a single shot idea. Models follow instructions more reliably in shorter clips; two beats in one clip is how you get mush.

concepts.name: The first frame anchors the generation
concepts.summary: In image-to-video the input image acts as the first frame of the output and establishes the visual starting point of the whole generation.

concepts.name: Shot sizes
concepts.summary: Wide establishes the space, medium carries interaction, close carries feeling. Coverage is chosen from the established space, not generated independently.

concepts.name: Motivated camera
concepts.summary: A camera move must mean something: a push says pay attention, a pan says look over there. Unmotivated movement reads as generated instantly.

concepts.name: Timed action beats
concepts.summary: Action is written as beats with timing ('takes four steps to the window, pauses, pulls the curtain in the final second'), not adverbs. Specific beats make the duration achievable.

concepts.name: Style anchored early
concepts.summary: The aesthetic ('1970s film', '16mm black-and-white') is named early in the prompt so the model carries it through the whole clip; style drift starts when style is an afterthought.

concepts.name: Character consistency by reference, not adjectives
concepts.summary: Identity holds through pictures: character reference uploads (Sora), up to three reference images (Veo 3.1), elements (Kling). Prose descriptions drift; references are reused verbatim.

concepts.name: Seeds are a weak consistency tool
concepts.summary: A fixed seed nudges similar style and motion where supported (Runway offers it, off by default), but a seed names a draw, not a reproducible output; hosted endpoints do not guarantee the same result.

concepts.name: The capability map is dated
concepts.summary: As of 2026-09-26: Runway Gen-4 makes 5 or 10 second clips from an input image with an optional fixed seed; Luma takes start and end keyframes and extends with an image; Kling takes start and end frames and warns that dissimilar frames cause a lens switch; Veo 3.1 offers extension, first-and-last-frame generation, and up to three reference images; Sora 2 offers character references, up to 20 seconds, and extension using the full clip as context.

concepts.name: Frame chaining
concepts.summary: The end frame of clip N becomes the start frame of clip N+1. This is the backbone of multi-clip continuity and the reason the last frame of every shot matters.

concepts.name: The lens-switch seam
concepts.summary: When start and end frames differ too much, the model cuts to a new lens instead of transitioning (Kling documents this outright). Big changes belong at a planned cut, not inside a chained transition.

concepts.name: The 180-degree axis
concepts.summary: Screen direction is a promise: keep the camera on one side of the action line between chained clips unless the disorientation is intentional.

concepts.name: Establish before coverage
concepts.summary: The wide shot comes first so the space exists; mediums and close-ups must agree with it, or the viewer rebuilds the room wrong.

concepts.name: Cut on action
concepts.summary: Motion continuing across a cut hides the seam. The safest moment to join two clips is mid-gesture, not at rest.

concepts.name: Stitch short beats over generating long
concepts.summary: Two planned 4-second clips edited together routinely beat one asked-for 8-second clip when the action is complex; OpenAI's own guide recommends exactly this.

concepts.name: Lighting and palette continuity
concepts.summary: Time of day, light direction, and palette are named identically across every clip's prompt and reference, or each generation re-lights the scene.

concepts.name: The shot list is a written artifact
concepts.summary: A sequence is planned as a written shot list (framing, beat, camera, duration, references per shot) before any generation, so continuity is designed rather than hoped for.

misconceptions.claim: A longer, more detailed prompt gives more control.
misconceptions.correction: Duration, resolution and aspect are parameters; prose cannot change them, and models follow instructions more reliably in shorter clips.

misconceptions.claim: Locking the seed makes a generation reproducible.
misconceptions.correction: Where offered, a fixed seed only nudges similar style and motion; a seed names a draw, not a guarantee, and hosted endpoints do not promise bit-identical reruns.

misconceptions.claim: Describing the character the same way every time keeps them consistent.
misconceptions.correction: Consistent phrasing helps but drifts; identity holds through reference images uploaded once and reused.

misconceptions.claim: One long generation is better than stitching short clips.
misconceptions.correction: For complex action the opposite holds: stitch planned short clips, ideally cutting on motion.

misconceptions.claim: Any two frames can be bridged with a start/end-frame tool.
misconceptions.correction: Frames that differ too much produce a lens switch, not a transition; big changes belong at a planned cut.

edgeCases.case: A generator with no start/end-frame support: chaining degrades to extracting the last frame yourself and feeding it as the next input image.
Vertical versus landscape decided late: some paths (Veo Ingredients) now generate native vertical, so format is a container decision made per clip, not in the edit.
A shot whose action cannot fit its duration: the fix is a smaller beat or a cut, not a longer duration request in prose.
Reference images that disagree with each other: Veo takes up to three; conflicting references produce a blend of identities.

realWorldFailures.failure: The character's face, wardrobe, or age drifts between clip 1 and clip 3 of the same story.
realWorldFailures.lesson: Identity comes from reused reference images, not repeated prose.

realWorldFailures.failure: A chained transition cuts to a new lens halfway through because the two frames were too different.
realWorldFailures.lesson: Keep chained frames similar; put big changes at a planned cut.

realWorldFailures.failure: The camera drifts and wanders through every clip, reading as unmistakably AI.
realWorldFailures.lesson: Static or motivated camera only; every move needs a reason.

realWorldFailures.failure: One 10-second clip asked to carry a walk in, a conversation, and a reveal comes back as mush.
realWorldFailures.lesson: One beat per clip; complex action gets stitched from planned short clips.
